claims.text: Richard Wagner (1813-1883) was a German composer who moved to Bayreuth in 1872 to oversee the building of a festival theatre for his operas. Nietzsche was for some years his friend and admirer.

citations.title: Richard Wagner in Bayreuth (course notes)
citations.quote: the Wagners moved to distant Bayreuth to oversee the building of the Festspielhaus in April 1872.

claims.text: Nietzsche last saw the Wagners in November 1876, after which he turned against him.

citations.title: Richard Wagner in Bayreuth (course notes)
citations.quote: In November of 1876, Nietzsche saw the Wagners for the last time.

items.heading: Wagner died as Zarathustra was begun

claims.text: Nietzsche wrote Part I in about ten days in January 1883, and Wagner died the following month. The course notes call his death another blow to Nietzsche, coming after the quarrel over Lou Salomé.

citations.title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (course notes)
citations.quote: Part I was written in only about ten days, in January 1883. In February, Wagner died, yielding yet another blow to Nietzsche.

claims.text: Nietzsche went to the laying of the foundation stone at Bayreuth in 1872, and he wrote the essay Wagner in Bayreuth to honour the festival opening in 1876.

citations.title: Richard Wagner in Bayreuth (course notes)
citations.quote: Nietzsche attended the ceremonial cornerstone laying, at Bayreuth, in May of 1872.

claims.text: The festival itself disappointed him, and by the time of Human, All Too Human Wagner was remodelling the Parsifal myth into a story of Christian redemption to attract Christian money to Bayreuth.

citations.title: Richard Wagner in Bayreuth (course notes)
citations.quote: Wagner was hard at work attracting bourgeois Christian money to Bayreuth by remodeling the Parsifal myth into a story of Christian redemption.

citations.title: Richard Wagner in Bayreuth (course notes)
citations.quote: I made the mistake of going to Bayreuth with an ideal in my breast, and was, therefore, doomed to suffer the most bitter disappointment.

claims.text: Readers commonly take the Magician, a false-seeming sorcerer whom Zarathustra meets in Part Four, to represent Wagner, Nietzsche's former friend.

citations.title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra: The Sorcerer (LitCharts)
citations.quote: The sorcerer symbolizes Nietzsche’s former friend, operatic composer Richard Wagner, with whom he’d had a falling-out.

claims.text: His wailing song is read as a parody of Wagner's poetic style.

citations.title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra: The Sorcerer (LitCharts)
citations.quote: The sorcerer’s wailings are intended as a parody of Wagner’s poetic style.
